title: Women's ordination
hook: the debate over full ordination for women, told from both sides with respect

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar and a movement that measured worth by deeds, not birth. Your line: a path of dignity. Whose name did you learn or use? Day one thousand forty-four.

Here's an odd thing about today's argument. Two people who disagree sharply can open the same text, the long account of the Buddha's final months, and each find a line for their side. One reads a warning about changing rules that were laid down. The other reads the Buddha naming who belongs in his community. The question is whether women can be fully ordained as nuns, bhikkhunis, in traditions where that line was lost. Today both sides get to speak, each at its best.
screen: `ONE TEXT, TWO SIDES.` → `A RULE KEPT AS LAID DOWN.` → `WHO BELONGS IN THE COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: As this path told some weeks ago, the Vinaya says the order of nuns began with Mahapajapati. Lines of fully ordained nuns continue in Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities, and those nuns are part of daily temple life. In Theravada lands the line broke, and Tibetan communities have had no unbroken line of their own. So here is the first side, at its best. Early in that long discourse, the Buddha tells his monks they can expect to prosper as long as they don't lay down rules that were never laid down, and don't throw out rules that were. The Vinaya says a nun is ordained by a sangha of nuns and then by a sangha of monks. For monks who hold this view, if the nuns' sangha is gone, no one now has the standing to make a new one, and inventing a way around the rule would be just what that discourse warns against. Keeping the form whole is how they keep faith with the Buddha. Now the second side, at its best. Later in the same discourse, Mara urges the Buddha to pass away, and the Buddha says he won't go until his monks, his nuns, and his lay men and lay women have learned the teaching. To supporters of restoring the order, that is the Buddha naming four assemblies, nuns among them, as the shape of his community. Some Theravada women have received full ordination with nuns from East Asian lines taking part, and some monks have stood with them. Notice what the two sides share: each is trying to be faithful, and each points to the Buddha's own words. The canon even has a talk for moments like this, the Kinti Sutta. When monks disagree about meaning, it advises going to them gently, showing exactly where the difference lies, and not letting it become a quarrel.
screen: `ONE SIDE: KEEP RULES AS LAID DOWN.` · `THE OTHER: NUNS AMONG FOUR ASSEMBLIES.` · `BOTH POINT TO THE BUDDHA'S WORDS.` · then, large: `NAME THE DIFFERENCE, NOT A QUARREL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: listen to both sides. Sit and settle. Pick a question you have strong feelings about, any question. First, for a few breaths, let the side you agree with speak in your mind, at its best. Then let the other side speak, also at its best, as its wisest supporter would put it, not as a cartoon. Notice what happens in your body as you listen. Tightening? Softening? You don't have to change your mind. Just let both sides finish their sentences. The bell holds the time.
Women's ordination. The question of whether women may again be fully ordained as bhikkhunis where the line was lost, argued by people on both sides who quote the same teacher. Today's word.
Your line: told with respect. Today, when you disagree with someone, try saying their view back to them in a way they'd agree with, before you give yours. Day one thousand forty-four.

howItsDone: Fully ordained nuns live and teach in East Asian Buddhist communities; in Theravada and Tibetan communities, women practice as novices, as precept-holding nuns, or in newer bhikkhuni communities, and the question is discussed by monks, nuns and lay people.

original.note: Pali parisā: an assembly; the Buddha names four, monks, nuns, lay men and lay women.

trapdoor: what you thought: an argument about whether women can be nuns.
what it means: a debate where both sides quote the same discourse, one for keeping the rules, one for the four assemblies.
what a scholar hears: DN 16's warning against changing what was laid down, beside its list of four assemblies, with the Vinaya's dual ordination in between.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): the draft retold day 1017 almost line for line (Mahapajapati at the gate with swollen feet, Ananda asking whether women can awaken, the same two sides, the same bhikkhuni original, near-identical match and myths). Rebuilt: the founding story is now one back-reference; each side is given its own text (DN 16 I.6, not laying down or abolishing rules, cited by traditionalists; DN 16 III, the four assemblies incl. nuns, cited by supporters), plus MN 103 Kinti Sutta on disagreeing about meaning. Hook, teach, screens, word, all games, original (parisa) and sources updated; older notes below about the gate scene no longer apply. Keeper: confirm both sides recognize their arguments, and the phrasing 'Tibetan communities have had no unbroken line of their own'.

Cullavagga X.1 paraphrased (Rhys Davids and Oldenberg's translation is public domain but not quoted). Details to confirm: shaved heads and robes put on themselves, swollen dusty feet, weeping at the gate (at Vesali), Ananda's question about women attaining the fruits. The number of refusals and the count of the 'heavy rules' (garudhammas) are left out on purpose.
'Who raised him after his mother died': standard tradition, confirm.
'Under special rules that placed the nuns in certain ways below the monks': neutral summary of the garudhammas; some scholars question their originality. Not raised here; Keeper may want a line.
East Asian lines (Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese) of fully ordained nuns: confirm list. Theravada line 'broke long ago': no date given.
Both sides are summarized in paraphrase with no names; confirm each side would recognize itself.

Tibetan tradition: 'women take novice vows, and teachers have studied how full ordination might be given': confirm; some Tibetan nuns have received full ordination in East Asian lines (not mentioned).
Teach screen heads label the two sides ('one side', 'the other'); 'Mahapajapati as its first member' follows the Cullavagga story.
